title: Auxin and Plant Hormones: How Plants Steer Growth

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Why does a seedling shoot or root bend toward or away from a stimulus?
cards.back: Its two opposite flanks grow at different rates. Light or gravity sends more of the hormone auxin to one flank.
cards.quote: A shoot or root bends because its two flanks, its opposite sides, grow at different rates.

cards.front: In the seedlings tested, does the auxin-rich flank grow faster or slower in a shoot, and in a root?
cards.back: Over the range of auxin these seedlings use, faster in a shoot and slower in a root.
cards.quote: Over the range of auxin these seedlings use, the auxin-rich flank grows faster in a shoot and slower in a root.

cards.front: How do plants differ from vertebrates in where hormones are made, and in the usual response?
cards.back: Vertebrates make most hormones in glands and carry them in blood. In plants many kinds of cell make hormones, and the response is often a change in growth.
cards.quote: in plants, many kinds of cell make hormones, and the response is often a change in growth
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: A {{c1::tropism}} is growth toward or away from a one-sided stimulus, and phototropism is one in response to light.
cards.quote: A tropism is growth toward or away from a one-sided stimulus, and phototropism is one in response to light.
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: Opaque caps over grass coleoptile tips stopped bending toward one-sided light. Why were transparent glass tubes over the tips needed to conclude that light is sensed at the tip?
cards.back: A cap might stop bending just by covering the tip. Transparent tubes also covered the tips, yet bending continued with the lower part lit, so darkness at the tip was what mattered.
cards.quote: Transparent glass tubes also covered the tips, yet bending continued, and the lower part was lit throughout.
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: Boysen-Jensen cut off coleoptile tips and set them back in place. Lit from one side, the coleoptiles still bent below the cut. What does this show?
cards.back: The bending influence from the tip can cross a wound.
cards.quote: Tips cut off and set back in place still produced bending below the cut, so the influence crossed a wound.
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: In oat coleoptiles lit from one side, mica (which dissolved chemicals cannot cross) is put in a cut below the tip on the shaded side in one group and on the lit side in another. Why is the lit-side group needed, and what result places the signal on the shaded side?
cards.back: Both cuts wound the tissue, so the lit-side group controls for wounding. Only the shaded-side barrier blocked bending, so a chemical signal travels down the shaded side.
cards.quote: both cuts wounded, but only the shaded-side barrier blocked bending
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: In Went's agar-block experiments on decapitated coleoptiles, what did darkness, removal of the coleoptile's own tip, and plain agar blocks each rule out?
cards.back: Darkness ruled out one-sided light; removing the tip ruled out the coleoptile's own tip; plain agar causing no curve ruled out the gel itself.
cards.quote: Darkness ruled out one-sided light, and cutting off the coleoptile's own tip ruled out that tip.
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: Went's angle could be measured, making a {{c1::bioassay}}: a measurement of a chemical through the response of living tissue.
cards.back: Went measured auxin activity, not the chemical itself.
cards.quote: Went's angle could be measured, making a bioassay: a measurement of a chemical through the response of living tissue.
cards.section: Bending toward light: what the controls ruled out

cards.front: Coleoptile tips lit from one side stand on two agar blocks, split by a barrier that stops short of the top. The barrier is now pushed all the way through the tip, so the halves cannot exchange anything. What happens to the difference in auxin between the two blocks, and why?
cards.back: It disappears. Auxin has to cross the top of the tip to reach the shaded side, which is what "moved" means.
cards.quote: Auxin has to cross the top of the tip to reach the shaded side, which is what "moved" means.
cards.section: Moved or destroyed?

cards.front: Sideways movement of auxin toward the shaded flank is the {{c1::Cholodny-Went hypothesis}}, named for the two botanists who proposed it.
cards.quote: Sideways movement of auxin toward the shaded flank is the Cholodny-Went hypothesis, named for the two botanists who proposed it.
cards.section: Moved or destroyed?

cards.front: How do cells set the direction in which auxin flows?
cards.back: Auxin leaves a cell through PIN carrier proteins. Many sit mainly on one face of the cell, so their placement sets auxin's direction.
cards.why: In the Arabidopsis hypocotyl, one-sided light changes where PIN3 sits, helping steer auxin to the shaded side.
cards.quote: It leaves a cell through carriers called PIN proteins, and many sit mainly on one face, so their placement sets auxin's direction.
cards.section: Moved or destroyed?

cards.front: In phototropism of the Arabidopsis hypocotyl, the light is detected by a blue-light receptor, {{c1::phototropin}} (first studied as NPH1).
cards.quote: The light is detected by a blue-light receptor, phototropin (first studied as NPH1).
cards.section: Moved or destroyed?

cards.front: A seedling is laid on its side, and auxin gathers on the lower flank of both shoot and root. Predict which way each organ turns, and why.
cards.back: The shoot turns up and the root turns down. The auxin-rich lower flank grows faster in a shoot and slower in a root.
cards.quote: Laid on its side, a seedling's shoot turns up and its root turns down, though both gather auxin below.
cards.section: Up and down: gravitropism in roots and shoots

cards.front: Where are the statoliths of a shoot?
cards.back: In the endodermis, a starch sheath around the stem's central tissue.
cards.quote: Shoots have statoliths too, in the endodermis, a starch sheath around the stem's central tissue
cards.section: Up and down: gravitropism in roots and shoots

cards.front: Wild-type Arabidopsis seedlings were inverted and the root-cap columella was watched. What happened, and what idea does it support?
cards.back: The plastids sank toward the new lower side, supporting sensing of gravity by the weight of dense statoliths.
cards.quote: the plastids in the root-cap columella sank toward the new lower side
cards.section: Up and down: gravitropism in roots and shoots

cards.front: What vertebrate sense uses the same physics as plant statoliths?
cards.back: The inner ear: dense crystals shift with gravity and bend sensory hair cells.
cards.quote: in the inner ear, dense crystals shift with gravity and bend sensory hair cells
cards.section: Up and down: gravitropism in roots and shoots

cards.front: Starchless Arabidopsis mutants have no dense statoliths. Grown in light and laid on their side, do their roots still turn down? What does the answer imply?
cards.back: Largely yes: they keep substantial root gravitropism. Statoliths are one gravity sensor, not the only one, and the other route is not settled.
cards.quote: Largely, yes: starchless mutants grown in light kept substantial root gravitropism.
cards.section: Up and down: gravitropism in roots and shoots

cards.front: The growing tip is cut off a shoot with strong apical dominance. Predict what the side buds below it do, and why.
cards.back: They usually start to grow. Losing the tip's auxin is part of the release, together with cytokinins and strigolactones.
cards.quote: In a shoot with strong apical dominance, they usually start to grow.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: What is apical dominance, and which hormone classes act in it?
cards.back: The suppression of side buds by the growing shoot tip. Auxin helps maintain it, together with cytokinins and strigolactones.
cards.quote: helps maintain apical dominance, the suppression of side buds by the growing shoot tip
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: What two main effects do cytokinins have?
cards.back: They promote cell division and slow leaf ageing.
cards.quote: Cytokinins promote cell division and slow leaf ageing.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: Transgenic tobacco made extra cytokinin in ageing leaves. What happened to leaf senescence, and which hormone effect does it show?
cards.back: Senescence, the programmed yellowing and death of a leaf, was delayed. Cytokinins slow leaf ageing.
cards.quote: In transgenic tobacco that made extra cytokinin in ageing leaves, leaf senescence, the programmed yellowing and death of a leaf, was delayed.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: Contrast the roles of gibberellins and abscisic acid in seeds.
cards.back: Gibberellins promote seed germination; abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant.
cards.quote: Gibberellins promote stem elongation and seed germination, the opposite of abscisic acid's role in keeping seeds dormant.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: A plant line has a mutation that blocks abscisic acid synthesis. Predict how its freshly shed seeds behave on moist soil, and why.
cards.back: In the illustrative results, they germinate with little delay. Abscisic acid maintains dormancy, a state of arrested growth in seeds, so without it dormancy is weak.
cards.quote: maintains dormancy, a state of arrested growth in seeds and buds
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: Besides seed dormancy, what effect of abscisic acid was shown in Arabidopsis?
cards.back: It induces stomatal closure.
cards.quote: Abscisic acid (ABA) induces stomatal closure in Arabidopsis
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: Tomatoes engineered to make little ethylene failed to ripen normally. Supplying ethylene restored ripening. What does the rescue add, and what is ethylene's role?
cards.back: The rescue ties the ripening failure to the missing ethylene rather than to another effect of the engineering. Ethylene, a gas, promotes fruit ripening.
cards.quote: Tomatoes engineered to make little ethylene failed to ripen normally, and supplied ethylene restored ripening.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: What do brassinosteroids promote, and what Arabidopsis evidence shows it?
cards.back: Cell elongation. Supplied brassinosteroids made up for the short, poorly elongated cells of several mutants.
cards.quote: Supplied brassinosteroids could make up for the short, poorly elongated cells of several Arabidopsis mutants.
cards.section: The other hormones

cards.front: Which light does each form of phytochrome absorb, and what does it convert to?
cards.back: Pr absorbs red light and converts to Pfr; Pfr absorbs far-red light and converts back to Pr. In the simple model, Pfr is the active form.
cards.quote: The Pr form absorbs red light and converts to Pfr; Pfr absorbs far-red light and converts back to Pr.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: Define a short-day plant and a long-day plant in terms of night length.
cards.back: A short-day plant flowers when nights are longer than a critical length; a long-day plant flowers when nights are shorter.
cards.quote: A short-day plant flowers when nights are longer than a critical length; a long-day plant flowers when nights are shorter.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: A short-day plant has a critical night length of 11 h. Does it flower on 12 h light and 12 h dark? On 15 h light and 9 h dark?
cards.back: Yes on 12 h dark, since the night is longer than 11 h; no on 9 h dark, since the night is shorter than the critical length.
cards.quote: Photoperiodism is a response to the relative lengths of day and night.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: Hamner and Bonner varied light and dark periods separately in cocklebur, a short-day plant. What two things did they report?
cards.back: Flowering depended mainly on the length of the dark period, and the leaves perceived the inductive treatment.
cards.quote: They reported that flowering depended mainly on the length of the dark period, and that the leaves perceived the inductive treatment.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: A short-day plant on long nights gets a brief flash of red light in the middle of each night. Predict flowering. In the model taught, what detects the flash and what times the night?
cards.back: It can stop flowering, depending on timing. In the model, phytochrome detects the flash and a daily clock times the night; sensitivity to the flash rises and falls with that clock.
cards.quote: a daily clock does, and the plant's sensitivity to such a flash rises and falls with that clock
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: In the simple phytochrome model, a mid-night red flash stops a short-day plant flowering. Predict the effect if a far-red flash follows the red flash at once.
cards.back: This is an extrapolation from the model, not a lesson result: the model predicts flowering returns, at least partly, because far-red converts Pfr back to Pr.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: Pfr is the active form, and far-red drives Pfr back to Pr, as in the lettuce-seed sequences ending in far-red.
cards.quote: In the simple model, Pfr is the active form.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: In Arabidopsis, CONSTANS RNA rises late in the day, and the protein is stabilized by light in the evening and degraded in darkness. Predict CONSTANS protein levels in short days, and the effect on flowering.
cards.back: Little protein builds up, because the late rise happens in darkness. FT stays low and flowering is slower, though this facultative long-day plant still flowers.
cards.quote: so it builds up only when days are long enough for that late rise to happen in light
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: What did Corbesier and colleagues show about FT protein in Arabidopsis, and what grafting result supports it?
cards.back: FT protein made in phloem moves to the shoot apex, including across grafts.
cards.quote: Corbesier and colleagues (2007) showed that FT protein made in phloem moves to the shoot apex, including across grafts.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: In the pathway taught, CONSTANS promotes FT transcription in leaf phloem and FT protein travels to the apex. If FT expression is blocked only in leaf phloem, what does this pathway imply for the apex, and what does the lesson leave open?
cards.back: Little FT protein would be made in the leaf to reach the apex, so the pathway implies the flowering signal is weakened. The lesson says only that part of the signal is known, so a flowering-time prediction goes beyond it.
cards.quote: CONSTANS then promotes transcription of the gene FT in the leaf phloem.
cards.section: Light as information: phytochrome, night length and a travelling signal

cards.front: An Arabidopsis triple mutant with almost no jasmonate was attacked by fungus gnat larvae, and applied methyl jasmonate substantially protected it. What does this show?
cards.back: Jasmonate signals defence against plant-eating animals in this system.
cards.quote: a triple mutant with almost no jasmonate was attacked by larvae of the fungus gnat Bradysia impatiens
cards.section: Signals of attack

cards.front: What is systemic acquired resistance, and which hormone works in it?
cards.back: An infection in one part of a plant leaves uninfected parts more resistant to later attack. Salicylic acid works in it.
cards.quote: Salicylic acid works in systemic acquired resistance, in which an infection in one part of a plant leaves uninfected parts more resistant to later attack.
cards.section: Signals of attack

cards.front: Grafting experiments in tobacco tested where salicylic acid is needed for systemic acquired resistance. What did they show about its role?
cards.back: Salicylic acid is needed in the distant, protected leaves, but is not itself the signal that travels there.
cards.quote: Grafting experiments in tobacco showed that it is needed in the distant, protected leaves but is not itself the signal that travels there.
cards.section: Signals of attack

cards.front: Lettuce seeds soaked in the dark get equal flash doses: red alone gives 90% germination; red then far-red gives 15%. Predict germination after red, far-red, red, far-red, red, and explain.
cards.back: High, about 88 to 90%. The last flash decides: red converts the pigment to a form that promotes germination, and far-red converts it back.
cards.quote: Sequences ending in red give 88 to 90% germination; sequences ending in far-red give 15 to 18%, close to the dark control.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Lettuce seed flash experiments (one batch, equal doses, a dark control) show germination depends on whether the last flash is red or far-red. What can these data not show?
cards.back: They do not identify the pigment chemically, do not show other seeds respond alike (many need no light), and without replicate groups do not show how reliable the differences are.
cards.quote: The data neither identify the pigment chemically nor show that other seeds respond alike; many need no light to germinate.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a curvature bioassay, 200 degrees of curvature per mg per L of auxin. Split-tip blocks of equal volume give 6 degrees (lit half) and 12 degrees (shaded half). Find each concentration and the shaded share of the total.
cards.quote: Shaded share = 0.06V / 0.09V = 67%; lit share = 33%.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a curvature bioassay

cards.front: Same bioassay (200 degrees per mg per L, equal blocks): split lit tips give 0.03 + 0.06 mg per L. A block from whole tips kept in the dark gives 18 degrees. Does this support moving auxin or destroying it on the lit side?
cards.back: 18 / 200 = 0.09 mg per L, equal to the lit total 0.09. The total did not fall, so auxin was moved to the shaded side, not destroyed, as Cholodny-Went predicts.
cards.why: Assumes the blocks caught all the auxin and light did not change how much the tip made.
cards.quote: The total did not fall, so the result supports moving auxin to the shaded side rather than destroying it on the lit side
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a curvature bioassay

cards.front: Same bioassay (concentration = curvature / 200 degrees per mg per L, equal blocks). Split lit tips give 5 degrees (lit) and 9 degrees (shaded); a dark-control block gives 18 degrees. What do you conclude?
cards.back: Lit 0.025, shaded 0.045, total 0.07 mg per L versus 0.09 in the dark: about 22% lower. Moving alone no longer explains it; some loss on the lit side, or in collection, cannot be ruled out, and light changing how much auxin the tip makes is not ruled out either.
cards.quote: auxin concentration (mg per L) = curvature (degrees) / 200 degrees per mg per L
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a curvature bioassay

cards.front: How does auxin act inside a cell?
cards.back: It binds a receptor that triggers destruction of repressor proteins.
cards.quote: Inside cells, auxin binds a receptor that triggers destruction of repressor proteins
cards.section: Inside the cell and inside the root

cards.front: A root is bathed in an auxin concentration near the peak of shoot growth. Using the textbook growth curves, predict root elongation and explain.
cards.back: Slowed (in the textbook curves). The root's growth peak lies at far lower auxin, and past a peak more auxin slows growth.
cards.why: Rests on the classic curves: growth is not proportional to auxin, and root and shoot peaks differ. Why roots respond to so much less auxin is not fully explained.
cards.quote: with the root's peak at far lower auxin
cards.section: Inside the cell and inside the root
